For this concept, the LH tanks could be filled directly where hydrogen is produced and 2 delivered via trucks to the airport. Ideally, existing cargo handling equipment at the airport could be used to haul the storage tanks between a designated storage tank holding terminal and the aircraft itself (Airport Compatibility of Alternative Aviation Fuels Task Force, International Industry Working Group 2025). It is not yet clear how long the entire tank swap process would take and how much time, if any, it would add between aircraft flights. This refueling approach is still at a conceptual stage, so it is also still unclear whether the tank swapping could occur at a terminal gate and whether it could occur while passengers are loading/unloading the aircraft. For any of these refueling configurations, if liquid hydrogen were to spill, risks would include contact to skin and possible explosion. When the liquid hydrogen is released, flash evaporation occurs because of the high temperature difference between the ambient air and the liquid hydrogen at −253°C (20 K). In addition, the air surrounding the spill condenses to a liquid and even freezes very close to the spill (oxygen freezes at −218°C, and nitrogen freezes at −209°C). The combination of air condensing and the LH evaporating leads to a white cloud formation 2 above the spill (Friedrich et al. 2023). The rate of evaporation of liquid hydrogen will depend on factors such as air and ground temperature, spill volume, wind, and surface material. Only a few studies have looked at liquid hydrogen evaporation in detail (Takeno et al. 1994; Odsæter et al. 2021; Friedrich et al. 2023). These studies, as well as future studies, should be leveraged to create standard procedures to follow if an LH spill were to occur at an airport. 2 4.3.1.4 Aircraft Operating Procedures While it would be expected that most operating procedures remain the same with cryogenic- powered aircraft compared to conventional aircraft, some aspects will be adjusted. As noted in the previous subsection, refueling location may differ, which will impact how aircraft maneuver on the tarmac and the amount of time the aircraft is grounded between flights. With hydrogen as the fuel source, considerable water production is expected during operation. It will have to be decided whether water can be emitted while navigating the tarmac, especially in below-freezing temperatures (Airport Compatibility of Alternative Aviation Fuels Task Force, International Industry Working Group 2025).
